title: TA9-05795
frame:
Forum: Refugee Protection Division (first-instance tribunal).
Parties: the claimant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review: none; this is the first-instance decision.
How the layers nest here: The member of the tribunal is the author (layer 1). The claimant and the Minister make submissions to the member (layer 2). There is no earlier decision-maker unless the reasons describe a prior decision (layer 3). Testimony and documents are layer 5.

paragraphs.text: The principal claimant, XXXX XXXX, his wife, XXXX XXXX, their child, the minor claimant, XXXX XXXX, are citizens of the Czech Republic, and they claim refugee protection pursuant to sections 96 and 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).1 These claims were joined according to Rule 49(1) of the Refugee Protection Division Rules. The principal claimant was appointed as the Designated Representative of the minor claimant for the purpose of her claim.
The principal claimant fears persecution at the hands of the Skinheads.

The principal claimant alleges that, on several occasions, he was verbally and physically assaulted because of his Roma ethnic background. The claimants arrived in Canada on XXXX XXXX, 2009, and filed a claim for refugee protection on the same day.
The Panel finds that the principal claimant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection. ANALYSIS Identity
The claimants' identities are established through the oral testimony of the principal claimant and the supporting documentation2 filed. Issues of Credibility

The principal claimant stated that in 2007, he was attacked by a group of Skinheads. He testified that he was kicked in the stomach, and in the ribs, during the assault. A bus came by, and the bus driver started to yell to make them stop, or else he was going to call the police. The Skinheads ran away. The principal claimant stated that the police were called, that he described what happened, but the police did nothing because there were no witnesses.

The Panel asked the principal claimant if anything else had happened to him during the attack other than being kicked, and he said that nothing else happened. The Panel pointed out to the principal claimant that in his written narrative, Personal Information Form (PIF),3 he stated that that one of the attackers had a knife, and told the principal claimant that he was going to kill him. The principal claimant was asked to explain the discrepancy, and he replied that in his oral testimony he was focusing on the injury.

I reject this explanation. The fact that the principal claimant was threatened to death with a knife by one of the attackers is a major element of the story. It is reasonable to expect the principal claimant to have remembered in his oral testimony that one of the attackers had threatened to kill with a knife. The failure of the principal claimant to provide a reasonable explanation for this discrepancy undermines his credibility.

The principal claimant was asked by the Panel if he had sought medical attention as a result of this assault, and he stated that he went to see a doctor at a private clinic, and was told that he could return home because everything was fine. The doctor prescribed no medication.

The Panel pointed out to the principal claimant that he had not mentioned in his written narrative that he had sought medical assistance after this particular attack, and he replied that he could not recall why he had not mentioned it.

I reject this explanation. The principal claimant's written narrative is a detailed account of his experience in the Czech Republic. It is reasonable to expect the principal claimant to have remembered in his written narrative that he had sought medical assistance after this particular attack. The failure of the principal claimant to provide a reasonable explanation for this discrepancy undermines his credibility.

The principal claimant testified that, in either 2008 or 2009, he and his wife had gone to a restaurant in the city of XXXX. While there, a group of Skinheads swarmed them. They kicked the principal claimant, and one of his teeth was kicked out. His wife came to his assistance, but she was slapped by the attackers. The principal claimant stated that he and his wife managed to run out of the restaurant. The Panel asked him if he had reported the incident to the police, and he replied that he had not.

The Panel pointed out to the principal claimant that when describing this incident in his written narrative, he had stated that he was hit over the head with a glass, and not that he had been kicked. He was asked to explain the discrepancy. The principal claimant stated that he did not recall it because the attack was very fast.

I reject this explanation. There is a major difference between being hit over the head with a glass and being kicked. It is reasonable to expect the principal claimant to have remembered when describing this incident if he had been hit over the head with a glass or if he had been kicked. The failure of the principal claimant to provide a reasonable explanation for this discrepancy further undermines his credibility.

In his amended narrative, the principal claimant stated that, as a result of this attack, his two back teeth were broken which have been repaired in Canada. The Panel asked the principal claimant why he had not mentioned this fact in his original narrative, and he replied that he was tired and just omitted it.

I reject his explanation. The original narrative is nearly two pages long, single spaced. It provides details as to the incidents described by the principal claimant. The fact that the principal claimant had two teeth broken during this assault is a major part of his story, for it demonstrates the severity of the assault. It is reasonable to expect the principal claimant to have remembered that he had two teeth broken when describing this incident in his original narrative. The failure of the principal claimant to provide a reasonable explanation for this discrepancy further undermines his credibility. Counsel submitted a medical report indicating that dental work4 and a root canal was performed on the principal claimant.5 The reports do not indicate which teeth were affected by this procedure, or the reason for the procedure. Therefore, I give these reports little weight.

The Panel asked the principal claimant if he had called the police after this incident, and he replied that he had not. The original narrative also states that he had not called the police after this incident. However, at the beginning of the hearing, counsel amended the written narrative to state that the principal claimant had called the police after this incident. The Panel brought this contradiction to the attention of the claimant, and he replied that he had not called the police. During examination by counsel, the principal claimant stated that there had been a misunderstanding between counsel and himself with respect to this point.

I reject this explanation. At the beginning of the hearing, counsel specifically amended this part of the original narrative to read that the principal claimant had called the police. At the beginning of the hearing, the principal claimant affirmed that the amendments to his narrative had been translated back to him, and that they were true and correct. He did state that his counsel had discussed the amendments with him. He should have realized, when discussing the amendments with counsel, that the amendment with respect to whether he had called the police after this incident was not correct. The failure of the principal claimant to provide a reasonable explanation for this discrepancy further undermines his credibility.

The minor claimant was called by counsel, and she testified that while attending school she was, on numerous occasions, verbally attacked by other school children. She stated that other school children kicked her, threw her books around, and hid her clothes and shoes. She stated that she did report some of these incidents to the teacher who would reproach the students. State Protection

The determinative issue in this claim is state protection. In arriving at its decision, the Panel considered the issue of whether the principal claimant's fear is objectively reasonable. In order to do so, the Panel considered whether or not there is adequate state protection in the Czech Republic, whether or not the claimant took all reasonable steps to avail himself of that protection, and whether he has provided clear and convincing evidence of the state's inability to protect.
I have, already, made credibility findings with respect to the principal claimant's testimony as to whether he sought state protection.

As a result, I find that, on a balance of probabilities, the principal claimant has not established that state protection is unavailable for the claimant in the Czech Republic. There is a presumption that a state is capable of protecting its citizens. The claimant may rebut this presumption by providing "clear and convincing" proof of lack of state protection in their country of origin. The claimant must approach his or her state for protection, providing state protection might be reasonably forthcoming.6 Evidence that protection being offered is not necessarily perfect7 is not clear and convincing proof of the state's inability to protect its citizens, as no government can guarantee the protection of all its citizens, at all times. However, where a state is in effective control of its territory, has military, police and civil authority in place and makes serious efforts to protects its citizens, the mere fact it is not always successful at doing so, will not be enough to justify a claim that the victims are unable to avail themselves of protection.8 The onus is on the claimant to establish, on a balance of probabilities, that state protection is inadequate.9

When the state in question is a democratic state, the claimant must do more than simply show that he or she went to see some member of the police force and that his or her efforts were unsuccessful. The burden for the claimant to prove an absence of state protection is directly proportional to the level of democracy of that state.10 In an established democracy, such as the Czech Republic, the claimant must do more than merely show that he or she went to see members of the police force and that those efforts were unsuccessful. The more democratic the state's institutions, the greater the onus on the claimant to show he or she has exhausted all courses of action available.11

The documentary evidence before the Immigration and Refugee Board (Board) indicates that the Czech Republic is a functioning democracy.12 It has functioning political and judicial systems in place, and an official apparatus sufficient to provide a measure of protection to its citizens. Local failures to provide effective policing do not amount to a lack of state protection unless they are part of a pattern of state inability or refusal to provide protection.13 Therefore, a claimant must do more than approach one police officer unsuccessfully before deciding that state protection would not be forthcoming. There is an onus on the claimant to exhaust all courses of action reasonably available to him.14

The Czech Republic is in control of its territory and has functioning security forces, both military and police, in place. There is no evidence of a total breakdown of state authority in the country. Therefore, the burden of attempting to show that one should not be required to exhaust all avenues of domestic recourse is a heavy one.15 There are an estimated 47,400 police officers employed by the National Police.16

Counsel, in his oral and written submissions,17 argued that there is no state protection for members of the Roma ethnic group in the Czech Republic. I agree that, in the past, the Czech Republic has faced difficulties in providing state protection to its Roma Citizens. However, the documentary evidence currently before the Board indicates that the Czech Republic is attempting to correct its historical discrimination against the Roma people. I note, in particular, Board documents which show police recruiting programs aimed at recruiting from within the Roma communities that have taken place in both 2003 and 2007.18 Further, as many as 130 police specialists in the Czech Republic now deal, specifically, with issues of "extremism, racism and other manifestations of xenophobia."19 The latest report available to the Board indicates that the police in the Czech Republic now employ Roma Police Assistants and Minority Liaison Officers to help bridge the gap between the police and the Roma communities. Several police stations also report employing Romani police officers. This same paper states, "... in general, the police response to Roma complaints or calls of distress is equal to that of non-Romani Czechs."20

The principal claimant fears returning to the Czech Republic because he fears discrimination and intolerance towards the Roma people were he to return. Although documentary evidence indicates that violent attacks on foreigners and the Roma minority have declined since the 1990s, and remain largely out of the headlines,21 there is evidence that the Skinheads attack on minorities in the Czech Republic is on the rise.22 However, there is also evidence that the state does not condone and, for the most part, does not acquiesce to this behaviour. For example: * In the mid-1990s, the Ministry of the Interior launched an initiative to combat extremism, allowing for police monitoring of extremist group activities and trends;23 * The government may prohibit gatherings, concerts, activities or speech which incite hatred and did so throughout 2008;24 * In January, police arrested 30 neo-Nazis in the Prague city center;25 * In October 2008, police countered a rally of rightist extremists who had arrived at a Romani settlement in Litvinov;26 and * In May 2008, police successfully prevented a major clash between anarchists and neo-Nazis in Brno, expelling the latter from the city, and in November 2008 the Workers' Party march in Litvinov police were able to break up the demonstrations, and in December 2008 the police prevented the far-right National Party from holding demonstrations in Brno.27

While there are concerns from some groups that there is impunity for racially motivated attacks, and the responses are not sufficient, the preponderance of evidence indicates that the state is taking action against extremists, and does not condone or acquiesce to extremist actions.

There is evidence that the Czech Republic is taking steps to assist the Roma community in several ways to ensure they will be able to participate in the Czech society. For example: * In January 2008, the Czech government established an agency for the social inclusion of Romani communities whose aim is to combat social exclusion and the formation of ghettos and improve the socio-economic conditions of Roma through improved access to employment and mainstream education;28 * The government continued its long-term integration plan for Roma, which was adopted in 2006 which provides for state-paid advisers to assist Roma in finding employment and special stipends for Romani secondary school students;29 * The Inter-ministerial Commission for Romani Community Affairs, coordinated by the minister for human rights and minorities, included 12 government and 14 Romani representatives, as well as the ombudsman; it continued to take an active role in resolving disputes between Romani communities and their non-Romani neighbours. The commission also promoted antidiscrimination initiatives in housing and education;30 * Police set up an information campaign to recruit minorities into the police force in Prague, Usti and Labem and Brno;31 * The government continued steps to address discrimination in the education of Romani children during the year. It continued the policy of closing "remedial" schools and transferring "slower" students into new special education classes or so-called "practical schools," pursuant to a 2005 law that abolished remedial schools;32

It is noted that critics claim these programs do not go far enough, or are just superficial. However, the preponderance of evidence is that there are programs in effect, and serious efforts are being made. This information further supports the finding that, while there is undoubtedly discrimination against the Roma in the Czech Republic, in this particular case, it is not systemic; the state has a variety of programs available to assist the Roma, and progress is being made in offering protection to Roma and their rights.

The principal claimant has not established that were he to return to the Czech Republic today, protection would not be reasonably forthcoming, or that it is objectively unreasonable for him to seek that protection.

I find that, on a balance of probabilities, the principal claimant has failed to rebut the presumption of state protection with clear and convincing evidence. As the issue of state protection is equally applicable to claims based on sections 96 and 97(1) of IRPA, his claim must fail.
I, therefore, determine that the principal claimant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection.
The Refugee Protection Division rejects his claim.

As the claims of the co-claimant, and of minor claimant, rely entirely on the evidence of the principal claimant, and no persuasive evidence was adduced to differentiate their claims from that of the principal claimant's, their claims also fail.

The Refugee Protection Division rejects their claims.
